title: Meningitis
summary: Practise a focused history in a time-critical presentation.

aim.text: Assess history taking in suspected meningitis in a young adult, recognising sepsis and the need for immediate antibiotics, and the public health aspects.

candidateInstructions.text: You are the emergency doctor. Ms Priya Nair, 19, a first-year student, has arrived with her friend Maya. Observations: temperature 38.9, HR 118, BP 100/60, RR 22, GCS 14. Take a focused history from both. Do not examine. At the end, summarise and state your initial plan.

items: Priya: headache since last night, now severe, light hurts, neck stiff, hot and shivery, vomited twice, very tired.
Maya: Priya was well until two days ago, worse overnight, drowsy and a bit confused this morning. A few small purple spots on her legs appeared an hour ago.
No head injury, ear or sinus infection, recent travel or seizure.
Lives in university halls, went to a freshers party last weekend, shares a kitchen. Unsure about meningitis vaccines.
No medical conditions, medicines, allergies or immunosuppression.
Concern if asked: "Is it meningitis? Am I going to die? Could I have given it to my friends?"

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Hello, I am Dr Shah, one of the emergency doctors. Can you confirm your name and date of birth?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Priya Nair, 14th January 2007.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Could you tell me what has been happening, in your own words?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: A bad headache since last night. I feel hot and shivery, and light hurts my eyes.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Thank you. Anything else?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: My neck is stiff and I have been sick twice.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Maya, when was Priya last completely well?

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.text: Two days ago she was fine. Last night she got a bad headache and fever, and this morning she was drowsy and confused.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any rash?

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.text: A few small purple spots on her legs, starting an hour ago.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Priya, any fits, or a head injury?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No fits, no head injury.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any ear or sinus infection, travel, or contact with someone with meningitis? Where do you live?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I live in halls, and there was a big party last weekend.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Have you had the meningitis vaccines? Any conditions, medicines or allergies?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I am not sure about the vaccines. No conditions, no medicines, no allergies.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: What worries you most?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Is it meningitis? Am I going to die? Could I have given it to my friends?

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: I understand. This could be meningitis or blood poisoning, and we treat it as an emergency. To summarise, you have had fever, severe headache, a stiff neck, light sensitivity, vomiting and drowsiness since last night, with a new purple rash, and you live in halls. I am giving you antibiotics through a drip straight away, taking blood tests and giving fluids, and the senior doctor will see you now. A scan or a back needle test may follow. We will also tell public health, who will look after your close contacts. Any questions?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No, please hurry.

head: Task
Expected in this station
rows: Do
Introduce yourself, check name and date of birth, start with an open question, listen, signpost, summarise and state a plan.
Find

Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting and drowsiness since last night, new non-blanching purple spots, university halls and recent party, unsure of vaccination, not immunosuppressed.
Ask
Time course, rash, neck stiffness, photophobia, confusion, fits, head injury, ear or sinus infection, travel, contacts, vaccination, immunosuppression, medicines, allergies.
Manage
Say aloud: sepsis pathway, blood cultures, immediate IV ceftriaxone, fluids, glucose, lactate, senior and critical care review, CT before LP only if indicated, notify public health.
React
Acknowledge fear, stay calm, do not falsely reassure, say you would ask the senior when unsure.

head: Situation
Good response
rows: Patient becomes drowsier
Recheck ABCDE and GCS, call critical care, do not delay antibiotics.
Friend is worried about spreading it
Reassure, explain public health will advise close contacts about preventive antibiotics.
Asked to wait for the scan first
Explain that antibiotics come first and the scan follows if needed.

head: Medical term
Say instead
rows: Meningitis
Infection of the lining around the brain and spinal cord
Septicaemia
Infection in the blood
Photophobia
Light hurting the eyes
Non-blanching rash
Spots that do not fade when pressed
Lumbar puncture
A needle test in the lower back to take fluid
Prophylaxis
Preventive antibiotics for close contacts

head: Question
Model reply
rows: Is it meningitis?
"It could be. We are treating you straight away without waiting for tests."
Am I going to die?
"This is serious, and we are acting very quickly, which gives you the best chance."
Could I have infected my friends?
"Public health will contact close contacts and give preventive advice."
Why antibiotics before the scan?
"Every hour counts. The scan will not change what we give first."

patientQuestions.text: Tips: acknowledge the feeling first, short sentences, check understanding, no false reassurance.

items: Sepsis approach: oxygen, IV access, blood cultures, lactate, glucose, fluids.
Immediate IV ceftriaxone. Do not delay for CT or lumbar puncture.
Dexamethasone per local guidance, early senior and critical care review, consider aciclovir if encephalitis is possible.

examinerQuestions.question: When must you scan before a lumbar puncture?

items: Reduced GCS, focal neurology, new seizures, papilloedema, immunocompromise, or signs of raised intracranial pressure.
Never delay antibiotics. Send blood PCR, and perform the LP when safe.

examinerQuestions.question: What does the non-blanching rash suggest?

items: Meningococcal septicaemia: an emergency.
Give antibiotics immediately and call for senior help. Use the glass test.

examinerQuestions.question: What public health steps are needed?

items: Notify the local health protection team.
Close contacts may need preventive antibiotics and vaccination advice.
Droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective treatment.

items: Delaying antibiotics for a scan or lumbar puncture.
Missing the rash, or not asking about vaccination and contacts.
No senior escalation or sepsis plan.
No summary or plan, or jargon without explanation.
Antibiotics first, tests second.
